reverse_outline.summary: Preview of what the introduction covers: readership, argument, failure patterns, scale stages, the fictional merchant, structure, routing, scope limits and evidence
Three key points: platform as promise-keeper, failures arise at joins between systems, architecture assigns who promises and resolves disagreement across scale stages
Opening scene: a shopper places an order with the fictional brand and the merchant's systems must now fulfil it
The order carries several promises, each depending on a different system, so a stale answer can make checkout commit to something unkeepable
Black Friday oversell example: systems stayed up but stale stock copies caused failed handoffs
What the book does: follows the order end to end for newcomers, covering ownership, change propagation and conflicts as the merchant grows, with reading options
Target readers new to commerce architecture, by kind of organization or role they have joined
Assumed prior knowledge: basic software concepts, no commerce background
Terms are defined where needed in each chapter and gathered in a glossary
Author's stance as an advising architect, with first-person judgements and stated conditions
Redefining 'commerce platform' as the full set of systems that make and keep customer promises, enumerated
Promises are made in one system and kept in others, linked by fallible handoffs
Central claim that failures live in joins, illustrated by three named incidents (oversell, three-status order, double refund)
Lead-in to the three questions architecture answers for each promise
Names of the sixteen failure patterns, grouped into four families
Patterns cascade into one another, Black Friday combined two, and chapters tag the patterns they address

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The intro reader predicted the expected order (who; argument; failure patterns; stages and merchant; organization along the order; finding a chapter and what is left to others; evidence and currency) and named one fictional order and one fictional incident as the evidence.
Every outline summary agrees with the controlling idea of its aligned spec paragraph, in the spec's order; structure check also passes.
The outliner marked no unit as carrying two ideas.

Every unit traces to S1-S5: audience (S1), argument and patterns (S2), stages and merchant (S3), layout, routing and scope (S4), evidence, sources and limits (S5); the conclusion restates the thesis question.

Figures 1 and 2 have explanatory captions and surrounding prose; each table (three questions, stages, parts, routing, kinds of statement, tiers) is introduced and followed by text that says how to read it; the dated Zalando, bol, Shopify and Omnibus facts each carry the point they make.

results.quote: **Why claims carry dates.** An undated claim quietly goes stale.
results.finding: The declared carry-over is the documented fact written with its year in the sentence, but that rule sits in the kinds-of-statement table two units back; the unit before this boundary ends on recommendations ('still a recommendation, with reasons and exceptions'), so the additional-support link to 'the year in the sentence' is not carried at the boundary. The declared order (p26 between the table and p27) causes it.
Every does_not_know term used on the page is glossed at first use: SKU, system of record, idempotency, EDI, WMS, PIM, ERP, 3PL, channels, reconciliation; no flow reader reported an unexplained term.

results.quote: The book calls that incident the Three-Status Order: three honest systems describing three different objects
results.finding: Both readers re-read because the incident names (Three-Status Order, Double Refund) and the pattern names one section later (Schrödinger's Order, The Boomerang) are never matched; flow-A: 'Two sets of names for related things in adjacent sections made me go back.'
results.corroborated_by: flow-B: item 2, same mismatch of incident and pattern names

results.quote: Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday 2026 met two at once:
results.finding: Both readers took the Black Friday sentence as the end of the chain just described and re-read to see that First Snowfall is outside it; flow-A: 'I re-read the paragraph to see whether First Snowfall was part of the chain. It is not, but the paragraph does not say so.'

results.quote: Where Parts II to V take the journey one step at a time, the four journeys of Part IX run it whole.
results.finding: This contradicts ¶3 ('Parts II to IV follow the order ...; Part V brings in the orders that arrive from marketplaces'), and both readers stopped to check whether Part V is on the journey; the spec's p22 controlling idea itself says 'Parts II to V'.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B: item 6, same II-IV vs II-V conflict

results.quote: a decision copied from a bigger company or carried out all at once on a single day
results.finding: flow-A: 'On first reading I could not tell which half of this description applies to which pattern. The First Snowfall becomes clear only two paragraphs later.'

results.quote: Each one takes a Kestrel & Pine story with fixed dates and amounts and runs it twice: through the January 2027 architecture, before Waypoint, and through the late-2027 one, after it.
results.finding: flow-A paused to work out that the late-2027 run is a replay of stories (Black Friday 2026, Eva's April order) that happened before Waypoint landed: 'resolves it, but only after a re-read.'

results.quote: Another Kestrel & Pine order showed *Delivered* on the platform, *In picking* (still being collected from the shelves) in the warehouse and *Not invoiced* in the ERP for six days.
results.finding: flow-B re-read: a parcel delivered while still being picked seemed impossible until the next sentence, and it stayed unclear whether the order had several lines and what 'for six days' applies to.

results.quote: Behind Eva's promises stands what is usually called a commerce platform, described as a product you subscribe to, license or assemble.
results.finding: flow-B: the long list of systems after the colon made the reader lose the definition's main clause and re-read to find where the definition ended.

results.quote: The parts, the routing table, the stage tables and the kinds of statement all ask of a promise which system makes it, which keeps it and how far the answer holds for a business of your shape.
results.finding: flow-B re-read: the kinds of statement weigh a sentence and do not ask which system makes a promise, so the synthesis list feels forced; the spec's p46 controlling idea and conclusion synthesis declare that list.
The opening is a vivid anecdote (Eva's order, then the Black Friday incident) leading to the claim; none of the weak introduction patterns.
The conclusion gives next steps for both readers and one question to carry; no weak conclusion pattern.
Where to Go Next ties parts, routing table, stages and kinds of statement to one question and states the so-what: ask which system keeps a promise before asking which product to buy.
The five promises from Eva's order return as 'this jacket, at this price, in stock, on Thursday, returnable'.
The reader stated the promise-keeping argument and listed the parts' subjects in order from the table, matching the expected answer.
The reader named the inventory and availability chapter and quoted the reason (ownership of stock, not faster copies), with systems of record and reconciliation next.
The reader labelled (a) illustration, (b) recommendation, (c) assumption, with the page's reasons.
The reader gave the page's definitions of SKU, system of record and idempotency, matching the expected answer.
The reader placed the brand at Omnichannel because shape decides the stage and revenue bands are markers, quoting the page.
The reader answered no on both counts: the models are maps inferred from public behavior, real companies appear as dated cases, and the book recommends architectures, not products.
